# Executive Summary 

414 Insurance's dataset with depression data can reveal key characteristics as early mental illness predictors. Being able to quickly identify at-risk patients is an important priority for 414 Insurance, as it leads to preventions of the most extreme mental illness scenarios. 

We use data-forward methodologies to assess mental illness patterns, recommending a targeted approach to predict onset of mental illness. Our approach utilizes supervised and unsupervised algorithmic learning models to find target characteristics. We demonstrate our work with each type of algorithm to propose the most effective strategy for identifying and preventing onset of mental illness. 

# Background

Depression--characterized by symptoms ranging from persistent low mood, loss of interest, sucidial thoughts-- is a common, clinically significant, and expensive medical condition for insurers. According to a Gallup poll, 3 in 10 US adults have been diagnosed with depression at some point in their lives ([Gallup](https://news.gallup.com/poll/505745/depression-rates-reach-new-highs.aspx)). In colleges across the US, 37% of the student population reported moderate to severe depressive symptoms in 2025 ([University of Michigan](https://sph.umich.edu/news/2025posts/college-student-mental-health-third-consecutive-year-improvement.html)). 

While there's a perception of depression as a benign issue, depression can cause difficulty maintaining relationships, work, or self-care. This causes it to compound into other chronic conditions, which increases total medical spending. In fact, 414 Insurance sees a 73% difference--a difference of $763-- between insurees with and without depression ([Health System Tracker](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/privately-insured-people-with-depression-and-anxiety-face-high-out-of-pocket-costs/)). 

Therefore, identifying high-risk members earlier opens an opportunity to target interventions before costs escalate ([Greenberg et al](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10499687/)).

The following links provide the detailed technical breakdown of our data processing and modeling pipeline.

# 1. Data Preparation and Exploration
## Main
The first phase of the analysis focuses on preparing the data for modeling. The raw dataset is imported from a CSV file and a random 10% sample is drawn to reduce computational burden. The Name column is removed as it carries no predictive value, and all character variables are coerced to factors. A preliminary inspection of the data structure and summary statistics is then performed. The cleaned dataset is subsequently saved as an RDS file for reproducibility.

* [Main Data Cleaning](Main.html)

## Initial Training and Testing Split
In the second file, the cleaned data is split into training and test sets following two parallel pipelines. The first preserves the original factor structure for tree-based models. The second converts the data into a fully dummy-encoded and min-max normalized format, suitable for distance- and gradient-based models such as KNN, ANN, and SVM. Both pipelines use a 50/50 split with the same random seed to ensure comparability across models.

* [Initial Training and Testing Split](trainingtestingsplit.html)
</div>

# 2. Supervised Learning Models
* [Generalized Linear Model (GLM) for Depression](glm_depression.html)

The GLM is our best individual model, with a Kappa of 0.143 and the most balanced sensitivity (43.8%) and specificity (70.8%). It correctly identifies a meaningful share of both positive and negative cases, making it the most reliable classifier among the individual models we tested. We believe it performs best because the predictors in this dataset relate to mental illness risk in a relatively straightforward way, and the GLM is well-suited to capture that. It also handles the class imbalance better than our other models without needing threshold adjustments.

* [K-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) Analysis](knn_2.html)

KNN performs poorly, with a Kappa of just 0.026 and a sensitivity of only 9.5%, meaning it almost entirely fails to identify individuals with a history of mental illness. On the surface its accuracy looks reasonable at 67%, but this is misleading: a model that always predicts "No" would score similarly. We believe the main issue is the class imbalance: with roughly 69% of cases being "No," the model's nearest neighbors are almost always dominated by the majority class, pushing nearly every prediction toward "No" regardless of the individual's actual characteristics.

* [Decision Tree and Random Forest Results](DT2.html)

The C5.0 decision tree degenerates entirely, predicting "No" for every single observation and achieving a Kappa of 0. The Random Forest does better, but only after we lower the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.34, which brings sensitivity up to 35% and Kappa to 0.095. We believe both models struggle for the same reason. The class imbalance is strong enough that neither algorithm finds it worthwhile to split toward the minority class without explicit correction. The Random Forest's ensemble approach gives it a slight edge, but it still falls well short of the GLM.

* [Support Vector Machine (SVM) Classification](SVM.html)

SVM proved to be the most inconsistent model in our analysis. Most of the kernels we tested (including the commonly used RBF and linear kernels) failed completely, predicting "No" for every observation. The splinedot kernel performed best with a Kappa of ~0.05 and sensitivity of ~0.30, and applying a lower threshold to the RBF model pushed sensitivity higher but introduced too many false positives to be practical. 

* [Artificial Neural Network (ANN) & Confusion Matrix](ANN-with-conf-matrix.html)

# 3. Ensemble Methods & Final Predictions

## Overview of Stacked Model Approach

The stacked model belongs to the family of stacked generalization (ensemble techniques) where a super‑learner (here, a decision tree) learns to combine base‑learner predictions in a way that can outperform any single model, strengthened by incorporating a cost matrix. 

In practice, each base model first generates a prediction vector on the test set, and then these predictions are coalesced into a single data frame along with the true response to create a new, smaller feature space for the second‑level model.  

### What is a cost matrix? 

In addition to combining the predictions of the five base models, the stacked model incorporates a **cost matrix** into the second‑level decision tree. 

In our context, falsely predicting that a non-depressed client is depressed (a false positive) may be an overuse of mental resources, while missing a depressed client (a false negative) creates large costs for 414 Insurance down the road. 

By assigning a penalty each misclassification, a cost matrix helps the decision tree optimize for a cost‑sensitive error tradeoff. 

## Kappa Analysis: Stacked Model

The stacked model achieved a relatively strong Kappa (9.81). 

It seemed like the stacked model mainly pulled from the ANN and KNN individual models. We hypothesize that since depression can exhibit complex patterns, the ANN was able to distinguish nonlinear relationships in the dataset.  The KNN contributes additional correlative relationships, creating clusters of similar depression groups that ANN  piggybacks off of.  This extra information lets the stacker better separate true positives from false positives, which shows up as a large jump in kappa.
